name: Ruy López
summary: Use 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 to pressure the defender of e5. Learn patient central play against the Morphy, Berlin and Steinitz defenses, with a practical plan for each.

chunks.title: Introduction: Pressure the Defender
chunks.summary: The bishop attacks e5's defender rather than aiming straight at f7. Learn why this creates useful pressure without winning a pawn immediately.
keyIdeas: Bb5 attacks Nc6, but before ...d6 this knight is not pinned: moving it does not expose the king on e8.
Bxc6 followed by Nxe5 does not simply win a pawn: after ...dxc6 and Nxe5, ...Qd4 attacks the knight and e4.
Develop and castle, then build the center. White can maintain pressure without exchanging the bishop immediately.

plans.white: Castle, support e4 and prepare c3 and d4 when appropriate. Respond to Black's chosen defense before following a memorized setup.
plans.black: Defend the center through development. Choose ...a6 to question the bishop, ...Nf6 to attack e4 or ...d6 to reinforce e5.

line.note: Claim e4, control d5 and open the f1 bishop's diagonal.
Black matches the central claim and frees the f8 bishop.
Develop with an attack on e5. The knight also controls d4 and clears g1 for castling.
Defend e5 while developing a knight toward the center.
Attack Nc6, the defender of e5, and clear f1 for castling. This is indirect pressure: taking on c6 and e5 immediately does not simply win a pawn.

comparison.explanation: 3.Bc4 starts the Italian, targeting f7 and controlling d5. Bb5 challenges the c6 knight instead. This is a choice of plan, not proof that one opening is universally better.

checkpoint.prompt: Can pressure on Nc6 win e5 immediately by exchanging the bishop?
checkpoint.answer: Not automatically. After Bxc6 dxc6 Nxe5, ...Qd4 attacks the knight and e4, so White cannot count on keeping an extra pawn.

questions.hint: Use the king's pawn to claim space.
questions.explanation: 1.e4 occupies the center and opens the f1 bishop. The intended Spanish setup follows with Nf3 and Bb5 after ...e5 and ...Nc6.

questions.prompt: Develop with an attack on Black's central pawn.
questions.hint: The g1 knight can attack e5.
questions.explanation: 2.Nf3 attacks e5 while developing toward the center and preparing castling.

questions.prompt: Attack the knight that defends e5 to start the Ruy López.
questions.hint: Develop the f1 bishop to b5.
questions.explanation: 3.Bb5 pressures Nc6. Bc4 is the sound Italian alternative, aimed at f7; Bb5 instead attacks a defender of the center.

chunks.title: Morphy Defense: Keep the Bishop Active
chunks.summary: Against 3...a6, retreat the bishop and follow a Closed Spanish setup. Understand why retreating can preserve useful pressure.
keyIdeas: ...a6 asks whether White will exchange bishop for knight. Ba4 preserves the bishop; Bxc6 is a sound but different structure.
After ...b5, Bb3 keeps the bishop on the a2–g8 diagonal while staying safe.
Re1 supports e4; c3 prepares d4. Black's ...d6 and castling support a continuing central struggle.

plans.white: Develop Nb1, often through d2, and prepare d4. Consider Bc2 and central piece coordination before attacking the king.
plans.black: Improve the pieces, challenge the center and consider ...Na5 against Bb3. A later ...d5 break, including Marshall-style ideas in other move orders, needs calculation.

line.note: Claim e4, control d5 and open the f1 bishop's diagonal.
Black matches the central claim and frees the f8 bishop.
Develop with an attack on e5. The knight also controls d4 and clears g1 for castling.
Defend e5 while developing a knight toward the center.
Attack Nc6, the defender of e5, and clear f1 for castling. This is indirect pressure: taking on c6 and e5 immediately does not simply win a pawn.
Questions the bishop before committing the kingside pieces. It also prepares a possible ...b5 expansion.
Retreats without giving up the bishop pair. The bishop still attacks Nc6 along the diagonal.

comparison.explanation: 4.Bxc6 is a respected alternative, exchanging the bishop pair for a changed pawn structure. Ba4 keeps the bishop and continued central pressure; it does not claim a material win.

line.note: Develops and attacks e4. White will need concrete central support or tactical recovery.
Secures the king. The Open Spanish with ...Nxe4 is possible; this lesson follows Black's quieter ...Be7 choice.
Prepares castling and chooses the Closed Spanish structure rather than taking e4 immediately.
Defends e4 with the rook. White can now build the center without relying only on tactics to protect that pawn.

checkpoint.prompt: Black's knight attacks e4 and has declined to capture it so far. How can White defend it with a rook?
checkpoint.answer: Re1 supports e4. It turns a tactical defense into a straightforward one and helps prepare a later d4 break.

line.note: Gains queenside space while attacking the bishop. Black uses a pawn move with tempo rather than a random expansion.
Preserves the bishop on an active diagonal. It still looks toward f7, even though it has moved several times.
Supports e5 and opens the c8 bishop. Black strengthens the central foothold rather than leaving its defense entirely to Nc6.
Prepares d4 with pawn support and leaves c2 available as a bishop retreat if needed.
Black secures the king and prepares to meet White's central expansion.
Controls g4 so Black cannot easily pin Nf3 with ...Bg4 when White plays d4. It costs a tempo, so keep watching Black's central options.

questions.prompt: Black attacks your bishop with ...a6. Preserve it while maintaining pressure on Nc6.
questions.hint: Retreat along the diagonal to a4.
questions.explanation: 4.Ba4 keeps the bishop pair and pressure on Nc6. 4.Bxc6 is a sound Exchange Variation, but trades the bishop for a different pawn structure.

questions.prompt: Black chose ...Be7 instead of capturing e4. Add a rook defender to e4.
questions.hint: The f1 rook can support the e-pawn.
questions.explanation: 6.Re1 protects e4 and prepares central play. Developing the rook has a concrete defensive purpose, not just a generic centralizing one.

questions.prompt: Black's ...b5 attacks your bishop. Keep it on the diagonal toward f7.
questions.hint: The bishop on a4 can retreat to b3.
questions.explanation: 7.Bb3 preserves the bishop. Exchanging on c6 now would allow ...dxc6, changing the structure; retreating keeps the Closed Spanish plan.

chunks.title: Berlin Defense: A Supported Anti-Berlin
chunks.summary: Black's 3...Nf6 attacks e4. Choose 4.d3 to support the pawn and keep a middlegame, rather than entering the main queenless Berlin line.
keyIdeas: ...Nf6 is active development with a threat to e4, not a passive attempt to defend e5.
d3 supports e4 and opens the c1 bishop. Castling immediately is also sound, but permits ...Nxe4 and different tactical lines.
After ...Bc5, c3 and d4 can challenge the center. Do not confuse this bishop on b5 with the Italian bishop on c4.

plans.white: Develop Nb1 and Bc1, prepare d4 and consider whether exchanging on c6 helps your specific position.
plans.black: Develop the c8 bishop, connect the rooks and prepare ...d5 when possible. Watch White's central expansion.

line.note: Claim e4, control d5 and open the f1 bishop's diagonal.
Black matches the central claim and frees the f8 bishop.
Develop with an attack on e5. The knight also controls d4 and clears g1 for castling.
Defend e5 while developing a knight toward the center.
Attack Nc6, the defender of e5, and clear f1 for castling. This is indirect pressure: taking on c6 and e5 immediately does not simply win a pawn.
Develops and attacks e4 directly. This is the Berlin Defense, and White must choose how to handle the threat.
Defends e4 and opens the c1 bishop's diagonal. This Anti-Berlin approach keeps the central pawn in place.

comparison.explanation: 4.O-O is a main line, not a mistake. After ...Nxe4, White uses central tactics rather than simple pawn protection. Our 4.d3 keeps a supported center and avoids that additional theory.

checkpoint.prompt: How can you answer the attack on e4 without entering ...Nxe4 lines?
checkpoint.answer: Play d3. It protects e4 with a pawn and gives Bc1 room to develop; immediate castling is another sound choice but leads to different positions.

line.note: Develops actively toward f2, adding pressure along the a7–g1 diagonal.
Secures the king with e4 already defended by d3.
Supports e5 and opens the c8 bishop. Black now has a firm center but still needs to develop the queenside.
Prepares d4 with support. White does not have to trade on c6 to justify Bb5.
Black secures the king before central play.
Adds another defender to e4 and puts the rook on a central file. White can continue development and assess d4.

questions.prompt: The Berlin knight attacks e4. Keep a supported center with the Anti-Berlin pawn move.
questions.hint: Use the d-pawn to defend e4.
questions.explanation: 4.d3 protects e4 and opens Bc1. 4.O-O is equally sound but allows ...Nxe4 and the main Berlin's tactical and queenless lines.

questions.prompt: Your center is supported. Bring the king to safety.
questions.hint: The path to g1 is clear.
questions.explanation: 5.O-O lets White prepare central play with the king secured. There is no need to force a bishop exchange just because Black attacked e4 earlier.

questions.prompt: Prepare to challenge Black's e5 pawn with d4 later.
questions.explanation: 6.c3 prepares d4 while preserving the bishop. Nc3 is also natural, but blocks this particular pawn preparation.

chunks.title: Steinitz Defense: Use Your Space
chunks.summary: Against 3...d6, open the center with d4, recapture actively, then finish development. Black is solid but has less room.
keyIdeas: ...d6 defends e5 but restricts the f8 bishop until it develops through e7 or g7.
d4 challenges the center while White's pieces are ready for central exchanges.
...Bd7 breaks the pin on Nc6. Before capturing, notice which pins have disappeared.

plans.white: Develop Bc1 and coordinate the rooks. Keep an eye on e4 and use the active Nd4 to influence central squares.
plans.black: Improve the remaining pieces and look for a supported ...d5 to reduce White's space. Exchanges can ease the cramped position.

line.note: Claim e4, control d5 and open the f1 bishop's diagonal.
Black matches the central claim and frees the f8 bishop.
Develop with an attack on e5. The knight also controls d4 and clears g1 for castling.
Defend e5 while developing a knight toward the center.
Attack Nc6, the defender of e5, and clear f1 for castling. This is indirect pressure: taking on c6 and e5 immediately does not simply win a pawn.
Reinforces e5 with a pawn. The d7 square is vacated, so the bishop on b5 now pins Nc6 to the king on e8.
Challenges e5 and claims more space. White's developing pieces can use the opened central squares.
Interposes the c8 bishop on d7, breaking the pin on Nc6 and connecting the queen to the center.
Develops the remaining knight and defends e4. White can meet a central exchange with an active recapture.

checkpoint.prompt: After ...Bd7, is Black's c6 knight still pinned to the king?
checkpoint.answer: No. The bishop on d7 blocks the b5–e8 diagonal. White should develop with Nc3 and calculate with Black's knight free to move.

line.note: Black relieves some central tension by exchanging e5 for d4.
Recaptures in the center with a knight, keeping the queen unexposed. The knight controls c6, e6 and f5.

comparison.explanation: 6.Qxd4? loses the queen to ...Nxd4 from the c6 knight. Nxd4 restores material with a minor piece instead. Notice that ...Bd7 has already broken the pin, so Nc6 is free to capture.

line.note: Develops and attacks e4. Black seeks active piece play despite the more compact structure.
Secures the king and brings a rook toward the center. Nc3 already defends e4.
Develops the f8 bishop and prepares castling. Black needs to finish development before further central operations.
Reinforces e4 and coordinates the rook with central pieces.
Completes Black's king safety. White should convert space into piece activity, not assume a forced attack.

questions.prompt: Black defended e5 with ...d6. Claim space and challenge the center.
questions.explanation: 4.d4 opens a central contest while White can develop quickly. Castling is sound too; d4 immediately uses the opportunity to gain space.

questions.prompt: Black's ...Bd7 broke the pin. Defend e4 by developing your remaining knight.
questions.hint: The b1 knight has a central square available.
questions.explanation: 5.Nc3 develops and protects e4. Notice that Nc6 is no longer pinned to the king after ...Bd7, so calculations must allow it to move.

questions.prompt: Black exchanged on d4. Restore material with your already developed knight.
questions.hint: Move the f3 knight into the center.
questions.explanation: 6.Nxd4 restores material and centralizes the knight. 6.Qxd4? loses the queen to ...Nxd4: Black's c6 knight is free to move because ...Bd7 broke the pin.
